findings.consequence: A prev cursor with a negative offset still raises AssertionError and returns a 500 in every paginator that inherits from BasePaginator. Forward cursors with a negative offset now silently return the first page instead of failing.
findings.explanation: In BasePaginator.get_result, start_offset is max(0, offset) only when not cursor.is_prev. For is_prev cursors it stays equal to offset, so a negative offset is still sliced. This is the same unsupported negative slice as before. The added comment says negative offsets are handled, but only the non-prev case is clamped. The change to the shared base class has no benefit for existing callers. For non-prev cursors it silently changes an error into offset 0.
findings.title: BasePaginator now passes negative offsets through for prev cursors, contradicting its own comment

findings.consequence: A request with optimized_pagination=true and a negative-offset cursor returns a 500 instead of a page. The 'advanced pagination' feature never works for the inputs it was written for.
findings.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, get_result calls queryset[cursor.offset:stop] with a negative start. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise AssertionError ("Negative indexing is not supported."). The comment claiming the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong. The offset comes from the client-supplied cursor string. The audit log endpoint turns this path on for superusers and global-access members who pass optimized_pagination=true. For such a user, a cursor such as 100:-5:1 reaches this slice and fails. The stop value is also wrong: it is offset+limit+extra, which can be 0 or negative.
findings.title: Negative-offset path slices the queryset with a negative start, which Django rejects

prs.title: Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs

findings.consequence: Any admin or superuser request to the audit-log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true that returns at least one row fails with a TypeError (HTTP 500). Following a cursor would also hit the wrong value type.
findings.explanation: The audit-log endpoint now passes OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime" when ?optimized_pagination=true. The previous paginator, DateTimePaginator, converts datetimes to and from numeric cursor values. The new class does not. Its get_item_key calls math.floor or math.ceil on getattr(item, "datetime"), which is a datetime object, so it raises TypeError. Its value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor.value, so build_queryset would filter a datetime column against a number on any page after the first. I read this from the diff and did not look up DateTimePaginator or build_cursor in the snapshot.
findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the audit-log datetime key and crashes

findings.consequence: A crafted cursor with a negative offset, such as 0:-5:0, returns a 500 error. If the slice did work, it would let callers reach rows outside the normal pagination bounds.
findings.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is set and the user-supplied cursor.offset is negative, the code runs queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. Django querysets raise AssertionError ("Negative indexing is not supported") for negative slice bounds. The comment saying the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong. The same expression is used for prev cursors in BasePaginator.get_result (line 180).
findings.title: Negative-offset slicing is passed to the Django queryset, which does not support it

findings.consequence: A trace with a parent chain deeper than about 1000 spans is flushed as several partial segments instead of one. Those segments are missing spans or their root span.
findings.explanation: The loop that follows the redirect chain was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`. The removed comment said this limit means trees deeper than the limit may not be joined correctly. With a chain longer than 1000 hops, the loop exits before it reaches the real set root. The span is then attached to an intermediate set_span_id, and the segment is split across several sets. The change cuts the limit tenfold with no stated reason.
findings.title: Redirect-chain limit lowered from 10000 to 1000, so deep span trees are no longer joined

findings.consequence: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, the wrong spans can be evicted. Duplicated spans are favored over legitimate later ones.
findings.explanation: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` uses the default AGGREGATE SUM. When the same payload is present in both sets, for example after a redelivered span, its score (end_timestamp_precise) is added to itself. The later `zpopmin` evicts the lowest scores, so it then treats that span as much later than it really is and keeps it over genuinely later spans.
findings.title: zunionstore default SUM aggregate distorts scores used by zpopmin eviction

prs.title: Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert

findings.consequence: After a hang, the hung flusher keeps running and a duplicate flusher is started on the same shards. This leaks processes. If the hung one resumes, both flush and produce the same segments, giving duplicate Kafka output and racing on `done_flush_segments`. Repeated hangs accumulate zombie processes. On join, live child processes are not terminated.
findings.explanation: Processes are created with `self.mp_context.Process`, where mp_context is `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`. That gives a `SpawnProcess`, which subclasses `BaseProcess`. It does not subclass `multiprocessing.Process`, which is `context.Process`. So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` at line 254 is False for the real processes. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. When `_ensure_processes_alive` detects cause "hang", the process is still alive, `kill()` is skipped, and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second flusher for the same shards. The old hung process stays alive. The same isinstance check in `join` (around line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either.
findings.title: Hung flusher process is never killed: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process fails for SpawnProcess

findings.consequence: After a hang, two flusher processes flush the same shards at once. This can produce duplicate or conflicting segment flushes. The orphaned hung processes leak, since each restart adds one and the restart count only caps at MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS. The old process also keeps sharing the stopped, drift and healthy_since values with its replacement.
findings.explanation: The old code called self.process.kill() unconditionally. The new code only kills when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process). The processes are created with mp_context.Process, where mp_context is the "spawn" context. That class is multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which subclasses BaseProcess and not multiprocessing.Process. The isinstance check is therefore False for real processes, and kill() is skipped. When cause == "hang", the alive-but-stuck process stays running. _create_process_for_shards then starts a second process for the same shards and overwrites self.processes[process_index], so the old process is orphaned. The same isinstance pattern in join() means processes are never terminated there either.
findings.title: Hung flusher process is never killed because of isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard

prs.title: Span Buffer Multiprocess Enhancement with Health Monitoring

findings.consequence: Monitor incident occurrences carry an unhumanized schedule_type in contexts.monitor.config. The intended display value is silently dropped.
findings.explanation: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config into a local `config`. It then replaces schedule_type with its display string, but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `config`. The local copy is never used, so the schedule_type conversion has no effect. The event context keeps the raw stored value, for example the integer code, rather than the display name such as 'crontab'.
findings.title: Monitor context ignores the computed config copy, so schedule_type is never humanized

prs.title: ref(crons): Reorganize incident creation / issue occurrence logic

findings.consequence: Any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` crashes `process_detectors` with a TypeError, so one such detector aborts processing of the whole detector list. Previously it was a harmless no-op.
findings.explanation: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty body (`pass`). StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract methods (get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data and others), and none of them are implemented. MetricAlertFire sets `detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler` (grouptype.py:27). `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (models/detector.py:86), so a detector of type metric_alert_fire raises TypeError ("Can't instantiate abstract class"). The old class implemented `evaluate` and returned `[]`, so it could be instantiated.
findings.title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an uninstantiable abstract class

prs.title: feat(workflow_engine): Add in hook for producing occurrences from the stateful detector

findings.consequence: A calendar or video failure during reschedule is no longer logged by the catch block. It becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which can crash the Node process or be silently lost. The reschedule flow also proceeds before the old calendar events are deleted. The same pattern appears in the bookings.tsx requestReschedule handler, which has no try/catch.
findings.explanation: getCalendar became async, so the forEach callback was made async. The enclosing try/catch (vital and wipemycalother reschedule.ts, around lines 124-137) only wrapped synchronous work before. A failure in getCalendar (for example the CalendarService constructor throwing, or a failed dynamic import of the app module) or in deleteEvent/deleteMeeting now rejects a floating promise. The catch block never sees it, and the code after the loop does not wait for the deletions.
findings.title: Async forEach callback escapes try/catch; calendar deletion errors become unhandled rejections

prs.title: Async import of the appStore packages

findings.consequence: If a caller omits `externalCalendarId`, `deleteEvent` falls back to the "primary" calendar. That is the wrong calendar when the booking's destination calendar is a secondary one, so the delete fails or hits the wrong calendar. `updateEvent` passes `calendarId: undefined` to `events.update`, so the update fails.
findings.explanation: The old fallback used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` when no `externalCalendarId` was passed. The change turned `destinationCalendar` into an array and replaced the fallback with `find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. That branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy. Because of that, the predicate compares each calendar's `externalId` to a falsy value. It matches nothing, or a calendar with an empty or null `externalId`, and the fallback always resolves to undefined. The same defect appears in `updateEvent` (around line 256) and in `deleteEvent` (lines 315-317). The code probably meant to use the main host's destination calendar, such as `destinationCalendar[0]?.externalId`.
findings.title: Google Calendar update/delete fallback to destinationCalendar can never match

findings.consequence: Creating a Google Meet booking for a user with no destination calendar throws a TypeError in EventManager.create instead of falling back to Cal Video. The booking creation or confirmation fails.
findings.explanation: destinationCalendar is now an array. In EventManager.create, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` gives undefined when the array is empty or missing. The next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining, which throws a TypeError. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was safe. The changed callers now explicitly produce `[]` when neither the booking nor the user has a destination calendar. These callers are confirm.handler.ts, editLocation.handler.ts and bookingReminder.ts. Any event whose location is MeetLocationType and has no destination calendar therefore throws. Before the change, such an event fell back to Cal Video.
findings.title: Google Meet fallback dereferences undefined when destinationCalendar is empty

findings.consequence: Collective bookings in that state create no calendar events on the other team members' destination calendars. The first host's lack of a calendar also stops the other hosts' calendars from being used.
findings.explanation: evt.destinationCalendar is null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destinationCalendar. The following `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` then does nothing. For a COLLECTIVE event whose organizer has no destination calendar but whose other hosts do, the collected teamDestinationCalendars are silently discarded instead of being used.
findings.title: Collective team destination calendars dropped when organizer has no destination calendar

findings.consequence: Orgs created without team billing have a null slug, so their org URL and subdomain routing break. Orgs created with billing get a live slug before payment or verification, which defeats the requestedSlug flow.
findings.explanation: The change rewrote `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` as `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, which drops the negation. When billing is disabled (self-hosted), the organization is now created with no slug, although the handler validated the slug and used it for the Vercel domain (lines 74-115). When billing is enabled, the slug is set immediately and `requestedSlug` is also stored. The old code kept those two cases separate: the slug was set only when billing was off, and `requestedSlug` only when billing was on. That separation is lost.
findings.title: Organization slug condition inverted: slug only stored when team billing is enabled

prs.title: fix: handle collective multiple host on destinationCalendar

findings.consequence: In serverless runtimes, the handler returning can freeze or terminate the process before reminder cancellation completes. Reminders for cancelled or rescheduled bookings may then still be sent, or their rows may remain. Failures are silent.
findings.explanation: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async (they call Sendgrid/Twilio and prisma). In handleCancelBooking the old code deleted reminder rows via prisma promises inside Promise.all. The new code calls the helpers inside forEach without await and does not add them to prismaPromises, so the handler can return before the cancellations and row updates or deletes finish. The same happens in handleNewBooking (lines 965-975). There, the try/catch cannot catch rejections from the unawaited promises, so the error logging is dead code. The helpers swallow their own errors, so failures are only console.logged.
findings.title: Async reminder deletions are fire-and-forget; reminder DB cleanup is no longer awaited

findings.consequence: Scheduled SendGrid emails for cancelled or rescheduled bookings are never cancelled, so attendees still receive reminders. The cancelled reminder rows are not deleted by this block. Their scheduled dates then pass and the earlier deleteMany removes them, so they are never retried.
findings.explanation: The file imports `client` from @sendgrid/client but only calls `sgMail.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)`. `client.setApiKey` is never called. `@sendgrid/mail` and `@sendgrid/client` keep separate client instances. So `client.request` to /v3/user/scheduled_sends is sent without credentials and is rejected (401/unauthorized). The single try/catch wraps the whole for loop, so the first failure is only logged and the loop ends. Remaining reminders are never cancelled. The delete promises already created are never awaited, because `Promise.all` is skipped. They can also surface as unhandled rejections. Nothing is retried per item. Even with valid auth, one bad referenceId (for example a null one) aborts the loop in the same way.
findings.title: SendGrid client never authenticated, so cancellation calls fail and abort the loop

findings.consequence: A single bad reminder can stop cancellation of later reminders on every run. Emails for cancelled or rescheduled bookings can still be sent, and cancelled rows stay in the table.
findings.explanation: The whole cancel loop sits in a single try/catch. The delete operations are lazy Prisma promises that only run at `Promise.all` after the loop. If `client.request` throws for one reminder (for example an invalid or already-used batch_id), the loop exits. The remaining reminders are not cancelled, and no delete runs, including for reminders already cancelled at SendGrid. The same failing row sorts into the same batch on every cron run, so it blocks the later cancellations each time. Those later reminders can then be sent after their booking was cancelled. The hypothesis' SMS concern is not supported. Only `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` in emailReminderManager.ts sets `cancelled: true`, and it only does so when referenceId is non-null. The early `deleteMany` only removes reminders already due or sent.
findings.title: One failing SendGrid cancel call aborts all remaining cancellations and the deletes

prs.title: Comprehensive workflow reminder management for booking lifecycle events

findings.consequence: If any other reminder method starts using `retryCount`, this SMS cron will silently delete those reminders, which loses scheduled notifications. If the update in the `catch` block throws, the whole run fails with a 500 and skips the remaining reminders.
findings.explanation: The cleanup `deleteMany` now uses `OR`. The first branch is limited to `method: SMS`. The second branch, `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`, has no method filter. `retryCount` is a column on every WorkflowReminder row, not only SMS rows. So this SMS cron endpoint deletes any reminder with `retryCount > 1`, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders. That includes reminders with `scheduled: true`, which already have a Twilio or provider reference. The default is 0 and only this handler increments the count, so rows from other methods are unlikely to reach 2 today. The scope is still wrong for an SMS-specific job. The update inside the `catch` block is also unguarded. If it throws, for example because the row was deleted concurrently, the whole handler fails and the remaining reminders are skipped.
findings.title: Retry-count cleanup clause in deleteMany is not limited to SMS reminders

findings.consequence: One failing or vanished reminder can make the cron endpoint return an unhandled 500 and skip every later reminder in that run. Those reminders only get scheduled if a later run succeeds before their send time.
findings.explanation: The change adds `prisma.workflowReminder.update` inside the `catch` block with no surrounding try/catch. If that update throws, the exception escapes the `for` loop and the handler. This can happen if the reminder row was deleted concurrently (Prisma P2025), or if the DB is unavailable, which is also a likely reason the original `try` body failed. The remaining reminders in `unscheduledReminders` are never processed, and the original error is never logged because `console.log` comes after the update. The same unguarded update was added in the `else` branch, but that one sits inside the `try`, so the catch handles it. The hypothesis's first claim is only partly right. When `message` is empty or `sendTo` is missing, the code skips without incrementing `retryCount`, so the reminder is re-fetched on every cron run. That is bounded, though. The `deleteMany` at the top removes any SMS reminde…
findings.title: Unguarded retryCount update in catch block can abort the whole reminder batch

findings.consequence: Non-SMS reminders that have accumulated retries can be deleted by the SMS cron. This removes them from their own retry handling.
findings.explanation: The new `OR` branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter. The SMS cron therefore deletes any workflow reminder with `retryCount > 1`, including email and WhatsApp reminders. Before the change, the delete was limited to SMS.
findings.title: Retry-limit delete clause is not restricted to SMS reminders

prs.title: SMS workflow reminder retry count tracking

findings.consequence: Existing attendees can receive a misleading "new booking" email with a fresh invite when someone adds guests, instead of the guests-added notification.
findings.explanation: sendAddGuestsEmails decides per attendee whether to send AttendeeScheduledEmail (new guest) or AttendeeAddGuestsEmail by checking newGuests.includes(attendee.email). The only caller, addGuests.handler.ts:168, passes the raw `guests` input, not `uniqueGuests`, which has existing attendees and blacklisted addresses removed (lines 74-78). If the input includes an email that is already an attendee, as long as at least one other guest is new, that existing attendee matches newGuests. They then get the full "scheduled" email instead of the "guests added" notification. The same applies to a blacklisted address, which is excluded from the booking but still listed in newGuests. Also, `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased but `guest` is compared as-is, so mixed-case blacklisted addresses are not filtered.
findings.title: Pre-existing attendees can be sent the "new booking" email because the caller passes unfiltered guests as newGuests

findings.consequence: An authenticated attendee can make the system email blacklisted or already-added addresses. Mixed-case blacklisted addresses are stored as attendees. Duplicate attendees can be created.
findings.explanation: The handler filters the input into `uniqueGuests`. That removes guests who are already attendees and guests on BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS. Only `uniqueGuests` are persisted. But `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the raw `guests` input. A blacklisted address, or an existing attendee, therefore still gets an "added to booking" email even though it was rejected and not stored. The blacklist check also compares the un-lowercased `guest` against lowercased blacklist entries (line 77), so `Bad@x.com` passes the filter. The input list is also not de-duplicated server-side, so repeated addresses create duplicate attendee rows.
findings.title: Notification emails sent to the unfiltered guest list instead of the guests actually added

findings.consequence: A single request can trigger a large number of attendee inserts and outbound emails, which is a resource-abuse and spam vector.
findings.explanation: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.max()`. The handler runs `createMany`, does a translation lookup per attendee and sends emails per guest, so the work grows with the array length. An authenticated attendee can submit very large arrays.
findings.title: No upper bound on the number of guests per request

prs.title: Add guest management functionality to existing bookings

findings.consequence: In mode 3, legacy writes are dropped or fail with context canceled. Legacy storage silently stops receiving creates, updates and deletes, so it diverges from unified storage. The failures only appear as legacy error metrics.
findings.explanation: The legacy write in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection now runs in a goroutine. Each goroutine calls context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) on the request-scoped ctx. In an apiserver that ctx is cancelled as soon as the handler returns, and the handler returns right after the method returns. The goroutine then usually calls Legacy.* with an already-cancelled context. The 10s timeout therefore never gets to apply. The goroutines also read the caller's obj, objInfo and options after the caller has returned. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) as the parent for the goroutine context.
findings.title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is cancelled when the request returns

findings.consequence: Storage errors are reported under the legacy metric. Dashboards and alerts show wrong data.
findings.explanation: When Storage.Create or Storage.Update fails (line 45 in Create, line 129 in Update), the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The failure came from the unified storage, so it should call recordStorageDuration.
findings.title: Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy durations

findings.consequence: The kind label gets an unbounded set of values, one per deleted object name, which inflates metric cardinality. Downstream logs also lose the name, kind and method values.
findings.explanation: On success, Delete calls recordStorageDuration with `name` where every other call passes options.Kind. Delete also builds ctx with d.Log instead of the enriched `log`.
findings.title: Delete uses the object name as the metric kind label and drops request-scoped log values

findings.consequence: Storage metrics are polluted with legacy timings and errors. Legacy delete-collection metrics are never emitted.
findings.explanation: The legacy goroutine in DeleteCollection calls recordStorageDuration with the legacy error and start time. It should call recordLegacyDuration.
findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy duration as a storage metric

findings.consequence: Any SQL expression query fails at parse time, even with the sqlExpressions feature flag enabled. SQLCommand.Execute and TablesList cannot work. This is a regression from the previous duck-backed behavior.
findings.explanation: enableSqlExpressions negates the feature flag (`enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`). It then returns false when that negated value is true, and returns false on the other path too. Every path returns false, whatever the flag says. ReadQuery's QueryTypeSQL case rejects any query when the result is false, so it always returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The flag-on case is never reached. The replacement DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go is also a stub: TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto all return "not implemented". The stub makes the real behavior unreachable and drops the previous go-duck implementation.
findings.title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so SQL expressions can never be enabled

findings.consequence: If a write event for a resource with no index arrives while init is logging, Go can abort the process with a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' error during startup.
findings.explanation: The change adds `s.search.TotalDocs()` to the init log line (search.go:216). It runs after the watch goroutine has started at lines 207-213. In the new bleve.go, `TotalDocs` iterates `b.cache` with no `cacheMu`. This change also moves the `cacheMu` lock in `BuildIndex` so that it covers only the `b.cache[key] = idx` write. A watch event handled in the goroutine can reach `getOrCreateIndex` and then `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache` under the lock. That write can overlap the unlocked iteration in `TotalDocs`. I did not read `handleEvent` or `getOrCreateIndex` in full, so the exact path from the event handler to `BuildIndex` is inferred from the excerpts.
findings.title: TotalDocs() reads the bleve cache map without a lock while the event goroutine can write it
